Incomplete, shared, or unverified KV states retain their native LRU order. 7 Evaluation We design the evaluation 3 3 3 All research reported in this paper, including access to and use of models, datasets, and code, was conducted by the university-affiliated authors. to answer two research questions: • RQ1: How does Coda compare with existing systems in throughput, SLO-compliant throughput, and latency across workloads and model sizes? • RQ2: How do routing, state admission, and execution admission contribute to Coda ’s performance, and what runtime behavior explains their benefits? 7.1 Experimental Setup Hardware Environment. We consider four configurations: ( i ) Setup 1: One NVIDIA A100-80GB GPU for admission-only ablation. ( ii ) Setup 2: 4 NVIDIA A100-80G GPUs, NVLink at 300 GB/s intra-node. ( iii ) Setup 3: 16 NVIDIA A100-80G GPUs across two nodes (8 GPUs/node), NVLink at 300 GB/s intra-node, InfiniBand at 50 GB/s inter-node. Baseline systems. We compare Coda with three baseline systems. ( i ) CacheWise [ 21 ] improves KV-cache reuse through prefix-aware scheduling and predictive eviction guided by tool-call metadata. ( ii ) SMetric [ 22 ] balances load and KV-cache reuse by routing each session’s first request based on load and subsequent requests based on cache locality. ( iii ) vLLM [ 13 ] serves as an unoptimized baseline using round-robin routing and FIFO request admission. Workload traces. We derive workload traces by subsampling TraceLab [ 30 ] at three request arrival rates, denoted Q1, Q2, and Q3, corresponding to 3, 5, and 7 requests/s. The subsampling procedure preserves the key long-tailed properties of the original traces, including the distribution of tool-call intervals. For single-GPU admission ablation, we use M1, M2, and M3, which contain approximately one quarter of the sessions in Q1, Q2, and Q3, respectively, retaining complete sessions with unchanged token counts and tool-call intervals. Models and metrics. We use Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-FP8 and Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8 as the served models; both are popular open-source models [ 25 ] . Each Qwen3-30B replica is served on a single GPU, whereas each Qwen3-235B replica is served on eight GPUs. Following prior work [ 21 , 22 ] , we evaluate overall throughput, SLO-compliant throughput, tail latencies for end-to-end (E2E) latency, time between tokens (TBT), and time to first token (TTFT), as well as prefix reuse rate and queue length. 7.2 End-to-end Evaluation (RQ1) We first examine whether Coda improves both serving throughput and latency. The subsequent ablations separate the contributions of routing, state admission, and execution admission, while the decision-level measurements examine how these mechanisms affect runtime behavior. Figure 11 : Throughput comparison for Qwen3-30B on Q1-Q3 under setup 2: output, request, and SLO TPS. 30B end-to-end throughput. Coda achieves the highest output-token , completed-request, and SLO-compliant throughput on all three workloads ( Figure 11 ). Relative to the strongest competing baseline for each metric and trace, the gains are 4.2-12.1%, 4.9-10.0%, and 15.9-44.3%, respectively. The larger gains in SLO-compliant throughput show that the improvement extends beyond raw token generation to output that meets the latency targets. For example, on Q3, Coda produces 642.1 output tokens/s and 103.2 SLO-compliant output tokens/s, compared with CacheWise’s 598.3 and 71.5. Relative to vLLM, the output-token and SLO-compliant throughput gains reach 56.9% and 70.3%. The advantage over CacheWise and SMetric further shows that the gains are not limited to replacing the unoptimized baseline. We isolate the contributions of routing and admission in Figure 14 . Figure 12 : Latency comparison for Qwen3-30B on Q1-Q3 under setup 2: TTFT, observed TBT, and E2E latency. 30B request latency (TTFT and E2E). Figure 12 reports TTFT and E2E latency, capturing request startup and completion, respectively. Relative to SMetric, Coda reduces p50 and p95 TTFT by 22.0-53.5% and 8.0-67.6%, respectively. It also reduces p50 E2E latency by 12.1-33.0%. Its p95 E2E latency is comparable on Q1 and 23.2-34.2% lower on Q2 and Q3. Relative to CacheWise, E2E latency is comparable or lower, with p50 reductions of 8.6-9.8% on Q2 and Q3 and a p95 reduction of 5.9% on Q1. Compared with vLLM, Coda reduces p95 TTFT and E2E latency by 66.0-68.6% and 36.5-43.1%, respectively. Taken together, these results show that Coda improves request responsiveness over SMetric and vLLM while maintaining comparable or lower completion latency than CacheWise. 30B token-delivery latency (TBT). Coda achieves comparable or lower TBT than CacheWise, including p95 reductions of 10.9-18.7%. Relative to vLLM, p50 TBT is comparable on Q1 and 11.1-17.0% lower on Q2 and Q3; p95 TBT is comparable on Q1 and Q2 but 6.1% higher on Q3. Compared with SMetric, p50 and p95 TBT are comparable on Q1 but higher on Q2 and Q3. SMetric’s lower TBT on these two traces is consistent with smaller effective decode batches: the decode-concurrency in Figure 16 is 13.0% and 22.6% higher for Coda . In summary, Coda combines higher throughput with comparable or lower TBT than CacheWise, while SMetric’s lower TBT on Q2 and Q3 accompanies lower throughput. Figure 13 : Throughput and E2E latency comparison for Qwen3-235B on Q1-Q3 under setup 3: output TPS and mean, p50, and p95 E2E latency. 235B results. Figure 13 presents the attainable performance of Coda on the larger model in a larger cluster. Coda achieves 11.7-18.3% higher output-token throughput than CacheWise and 3.1-7.2% higher than SMetric. Its mean and p50 E2E latency are 6.1-15.7% and 8.2-25.9% lower than CacheWise’s, respectively, while its p95 latency is comparable or up to 20.6% lower. Against SMetric, the mean E2E latency remains comparable, and the p50 and p95 latencies are comparable or lower by up to 11.2% and 14.3%, respectively. Overall, these comparisons demonstrate Coda ’s throughput and E2E latency advantages for the 235B model. 7.3 Ablation and Mechanism Analysis (RQ2) Figure 14 : Routing and admission ablation for Qwen3-30B on Q1-Q3 under setup 2: output, SLO TPS, and E2E latency. Component ablation. Figure 14 isolates the contributions of routing and admission by disabling routing optimization, admission optimization, or both. Compared with the routing-only variant, the full system gains 3.7-20.8% in output-token throughput and 12.1-17.3% in SLO-compliant throughput by enabling admission. Compared with the admission-only variant, enabling routing yields gains of 2.7-10.1% and 8.2-35.7% in these two metrics, respectively. With both optimizations enabled, Coda outperforms the variant with neither optimization by 4.2-33.2% in output-token throughput and 15.8-80.3% in SLO-compliant throughput. Its p50 E2E latency is also 12.1-33.0% lower than this variant’s, while p95 is comparable on Q1 and 23.2-34.2% lower on Q2 and Q3. These gains support the complementary roles of routing in shaping each worker’s request and KV-state composition and admission in controlling preparation order and attention grouping . Thus, the combined design achieves the highest output-token and SLO-compliant throughput across Q1-Q3 while maintaining comparable or lower E2E latency than every ablated variant. Figure 15 : Performance comparison on M1-M3 under setup 1: output, SLO TPS, and mean, p50, and p95 E2E latency. Single-GPU admission ablation. We examine Coda ’s admission performance in greater detail using single-GPU experiments ( Figure 15 ). Compared with CacheWise, Coda achieves 3.1-14.3% higher output-token throughput and 8.8-104.7% higher SLO-compliant throughput, with both gains increasing from M1 to M3. Against the shared SMetric/vLLM FIFO baseline, its output-token and SLO-compliant throughput improve by 12.5-35.2% and 104.4-190.7%, respectively, while mean, p50, and p95 E2E latency decrease by 27.3-39.0%, 44.9-55.6%, and 6.0-20.2%. Compared with CacheWise, Coda maintains comparable E2E latency on average across M1-M3; the equal-weight means of p50 and p95 latency are 3.8% and 2.4% lower, respectively. These results show that Coda ’s admission layer increases output-token and SLO-compliant throughput while maintaining comparable average E2E latency to CacheWise. Table 1 examines two successive admission refinements to the CacheWise baseline: Tiered-Aging state admission (TA; § 4.2 ), followed by Compatibility-Aware execution admission (CA; § 4.3 ). In addition to output-token and SLO-compliant throughput, we report useful throughput, which counts each session’s initial prefix once, appended input, and in-window output for completed requests, divided by the window duration. Compared with CacheWise, TA increases the equal-weight mean output-token, useful, and SLO-compliant throughput across M1-M3 by 6.9%, 1.0%, and 36.6%, respectively. Its output-token and SLO-compliant throughput are comparable to CacheWise’s on M1, with larger gains on M2 and M3. Adding CA while keeping TA unchanged yields further gains of 2.9%, 2.9%, and 15.6% in these three mean throughput metrics, respectively. The additional SLO-compliant throughput gain ranges from 10.0% to 25.6% across traces. The combined policy achieves the highest values for all three metrics on every trace, demonstrating the complementary benefits of state and execution admission. Reduction Q1 57 1.411 1.059 24.9% Q2 80 1.493 1.048 29.8% Q3 83 1.735 1.324 23.7% Total/mean 220 1.563 1.155 26.1% Routing-decision changes. Table 2 examines how context-length compatibility affects worker selection relative to SMetric’s reuse- and load-aware routing. During the five-minute measurement windows, Coda selects a different worker in 57, 80, and 83 decisions on Q1, Q2, and Q3, respectively. For these changed decisions, its selected workers reduce the mean context-length distance score by 24.9%, 29.8%, and 23.7% relative to SMetric’s choices. Across all 220 changed decisions, the pooled score decreases from 1.563 to 1.155, a 26.1% reduction. These results show that Coda ’s compatibility signal changes placement toward closer context-length matches , complementing the throughput benefits established by the routing ablation in Figure 14 . Table 3 compares Coda ’s admission choices and mean observed TBT with CacheWise’s. Within the five-minute decision windows, Coda makes 16, 37, and 77 different admission choices on M1, M2, and M3, respectively. Over the 10-minute measurement windows, its mean TBT is comparable to CacheWise’s on M1 and 15.1% and 14.6% lower on M2 and M3. Averaging the three trace-level means equally gives 69.06 ms for Coda versus 78.36 ms for CacheWise, an 11.9% reduction. These TBT measurements describe token delivery over each 10-minute window, not only requests with changed admission choices. Together with Table 1 , this comparison shows that Coda changes admission behavior while achieving higher throughput and lower average token-delivery latency. Figure 16 : GPU and KV-store hit rates and the mean decode-concurrency on Q1-Q3 under setup 2. KV reuse. Figure 16 shows the contributions of GPU-resident and KV-store hits to total reuse. Coda achieves total reuse rates of 88.3%, 82.1%, and 78.0% on Q1-Q3, respectively, exceeding CacheWise by 4.3-5.6 percentage points, SMetric by 5.6-11.6 points, and vLLM by 25.7-27.0 points. The source breakdown also distinguishes total reuse from GPU residency: on Q1, CacheWise has a larger GPU-hit share, but Coda achieves higher total reuse through additional KV-store hits. Coda thus achieves higher total reuse across all three traces by drawing on both GPU-resident KV state and the KV store. Decoding concurrency. The lower panel of Figure 16 demonstrates cluster-wide decoding concurrency. Coda yields 23.3, 30.2, and 37.5 concurrent requests on Q1-Q3, respectively. Its concurrency is comparable to SMetric’s on Q1 and 13.0% and 22.6% higher on Q2 and Q3, respectively. It is also 16.7-18.1% higher than vLLM’s. On Q3, however, CacheWise has a larger concurrency but lower output-token and SLO-compliant throughput than Coda . This comparison reinforces the importance of combining KV reuse with efficient execution rather than maximizing decoding concurrency alone. 8 Conclusion We presented Coda , a coding-agent serving system that exploits admission flexibility to improve serving efficiency while preserving request progress.
